nameStory: This tiny green alga is named after Gustaf Lagerheim, a Swedish botanist who specialized in studying algae in the late 1800s. The name 'Tetradesmus' comes from Greek words meaning 'four' and 'bundle,' referring to how these microscopic plants often group together in clusters of four cells.
description: Tetradesmus lagerheimii is a microscopic green alga that you'll never see with the naked eye - it's far too small! These tiny organisms live in freshwater and form small colonies of 2, 4, or 8 cells arranged in curved or zigzag rows. Each individual cell is spindle-shaped and incredibly tiny, measuring less than the width of a human hair, but together they play an important role in freshwater ecosystems as food for small animals.

idTips.label: Colony arrangement
idTips.description: Cells form curved, semicircular, or contorted colonies in single rows, sometimes arranged in a slight zigzag pattern

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: Individual cells are spindle-shaped or curved like a crescent moon, with both ends tapering to sharp points

idTips.label: Cell size
idTips.description: Extremely tiny cells, typically 9-34 micrometers long - you'd need a microscope to see any detail

idTips.label: Colony size
idTips.description: Forms small groups of 2, 4, or 8 cells clustered together in linear arrangements

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green coloration typical of freshwater algae, visible only under magnification

habitat: You'll find this alga in various freshwater environments throughout New England, including ponds, lakes, slow-moving streams, and even temporary pools. It's particularly common in nutrient-rich waters and can thrive in both natural and human-modified aquatic habitats.

seasonality.spring: Active growth begins as water temperatures warm, with populations building in ponds and streams.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when populations are most abundant and easiest to find in water samples.
seasonality.fall: Populations may decline as temperatures cool, but still present in most freshwater bodies.
seasonality.winter: Reduced activity in colder waters, but can persist throughout the winter months in suitable habitats.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, billions of these tiny algae can live in a single drop of pond water, producing oxygen and forming the foundation of freshwater food webs that support everything from tiny water fleas to large fish!
confusionNotes: Under a microscope, it can be confused with other small green algae, but the distinctive curved or semicircular colony shape and spindle-shaped cells with pointed ends help distinguish it from rounder or more geometric algae species.
contextualKnowledge: This species was previously known by the scientific name Scenedesmus acuminatus, so you might see it listed under that name in older field guides or scientific papers. The name change reflects modern understanding of algae relationships based on genetic studies.
compareHints: Compared to its relative Tetradesmus obliquus, T. lagerheimii has more distinctly curved colonies and more pronounced spindle-shaped cells with sharper pointed ends. T. obliquus tends to form straighter colonies with less dramatically tapered cells.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tetradesmus obliquus forms smaller colonies (2-4 cells) compared to its relative T.
